result.markdown: # Complex Data frame subsetting ![](/images/gear_2.png){style="width:200px; background:white; border-radius:5px; border: white solid 5px" fig-align="center"} There are many different ways to index __Data frames__. This page includes the following more complex topics: - Printing the top of a __data frame__ with `head()` - Subsetting all rows or all columns - Subsetting columns with the dollar sign (`$`) - Using __vector__ __functions__ with subsetted data - Using __data frame__ __functions__ with subsetted data - Transposing **data frames** with `t()` ## head() ![](/images/heads.png){style="width:150px; background:white; border-radius:5px" fig-align="center"} A quick __function__ to subset a __data frame__ is `head()`. By default it will return the first 6 rows. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #Return first 6 rows head(parks_df) #Return first 10 rows head(parks_df, 10) ``` ::: The __data frame__ is quite large. We will therefore use the `head()` __function__ and the __assignment operator__ to make the __data frame__ smaller for further examples. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} parks_df <- head(parks_df, 20) ``` ::: ## Subset all rows or columns ![](/images/columns.png){style="width:150px; background:white; border-radius:5px" fig-align="center"} To return all the rows of the specified columns you can leave the part before the comma empty. Similarly you can leave the part after the comma empty to return all of the columns of the specified rows. Leave both sides empty and you will get the entire __data frame__. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} parks_df[,] parks_df[,2] parks_df[3,] parks_df[,"State"] parks_df[2:4,] ``` ::: ## Subsetting columns with $ ![](/images/dollar_coin.png){style="width:150px; background:white; border-radius:5px" fig-align="center"} The sign `$` allows you to indicate which column you would like from the __data frame__. This is done like so: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} parks_df$State parks_df$Amphibian parks_df$Fish ``` ::: You will notice that the above commands return __vectors__. We can therefore subset these __vectors__ with `[]`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} parks_df$State[2] parks_df$Amphibian[2] parks_df$Fish[4:7] ``` ::: ## Vector functions ![](/images/park_award.png){style="width:150px; background:white; border-radius:5px; border: white solid 5px" fig-align="center"} Below are a selection of useful __functions__ that can be used on __vectors__. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #Sum the values of a numeric vector sum(parks_df$Mammal) #Mean of the values of a numeric vector mean(parks_df$Mammal) ``` ::: ## Data frame functions ![](/images/bison.png){style="width:200px; background:white; border-radius:5px; border: white solid 0px" fig-align="center"} The above __functions__ are useful but limted if you are working with __data frames__. Thankfully there are also many __functions__ used specifically for __data frames__ (they can also be used for matrices). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #Sum numeric columns colSums(parks_df[,3:6]) #Sum numeric rows rowSums(parks_df[,4:5]) #Mean of numeric columns colMeans(parks_df[,3:6]) #Mean of numeric rows rowMeans(parks_df[,4:5]) #Summary information for each column #This works for string and numeric columns with different outputs summary(parks_df) ``` ::: Try out some of the above commands with the entire __data frame__. Do they give an error? Is so, why? ## Transpose with t() ![](/images/transpose_table){style="width:300px; background:white; border-radius:5px; border: white solid 5px" fig-align="center"} Before we learn how to __write__ data to a file I will introduce one more __data frame__ associated __function__. `t()` which stands for transpose. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} parks_df[3:5] t(parks_df[,3:5]) summary(t(parks_df[,3:5])) ``` ::: Try the above commands without subsetting the __data frame__. What is happening and why? ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} You cannot transpose a whole __data frame__ which has columns of different classes.
